Repeated Glenn's 3-orbit profile; overshot landing target by 400 km

Aurora 7 was meant to be a repeat and became a scare. Scott Carpenter flew the same three-orbit profile as Glenn, but distracted by experiments and a balky control system he burned through his attitude fuel and fired his retros a few seconds late and slightly out of line — enough to carry him some 400 kilometres past his landing target. For a long, silent hour no one knew whether he was alive, until a search plane spotted him bobbing in a life raft. It is a plain reminder that in a machine with almost no margin, small errors compound fast — and that recovering from them is a skill of its own.

Scott Carpenter's 3-orbit flight — repeated Glenn's MA-6 profile to firm up confidence in the Mercury-Atlas vehicle before attempting the longer Schirra/Cooper flights. Carpenter ran extensive zero-g experiments and observation tasks; the heavy experimental load, a faulty pitch horizon scanner and fuel spent running the manual and automatic attitude systems together left the capsule ~25° off in yaw, and retro-fire came ~3 s late, overshooting the landing target by ~400 km. The recovery delay (Carpenter was found after nearly an hour and lifted out about 3 hours after splashdown) was widely reported and damaged Carpenter's reputation in NASA management; he never flew again. Capsule Aurora 7 on display at the Museum of Science and Industry, Chicago IL.
Atlas LV-3B from Cape Canaveral LC-14 1962-05-24 12:45 UTC.
Atlantic Ocean ~400 km past target; Carpenter found after nearly an hour and lifted out about 3 hours after splashdown. USS Pierce, USS Intrepid.
